subject: math
cluster: Understand ratio concepts and use ratio reasoning to solve problems
description: Students use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems. They build and read tables of equivalent ratios, plot ratio pairs on the coordinate plane, find and apply unit rates, and solve unit-rate problems including unit pricing and constant speed. They convert measurement units using ratios, and find a percent of a quantity as a rate per $100$. Reasoning tools include tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, and equations.
subSkills: Make a table of equivalent ratios and use it to find a missing value
Plot equivalent-ratio pairs as points on the coordinate plane and read values from the graph
Compute a unit rate from a given ratio (price per item, distance per hour)
Solve unit-pricing problems and decide which option is the better buy
Solve constant-speed problems relating distance, rate, and time
Find a percent of a quantity by treating percent as a rate per $100$
Find the whole given a part and a percent
Convert measurement units by multiplying by an appropriate ratio (unit ratio / conversion factor)

problemArchetypes.name: Equivalent-ratio table fill-in
problemArchetypes.example: A recipe uses sugar to flour in the ratio $2:5$. Complete the table and find how much flour is needed for $8$ cups of sugar. Answer: $20$ cups.

problemArchetypes.name: Plot ratios on the coordinate plane
problemArchetypes.example: The ratio of miles to gallons is $30:1$. Plot the points $(1,30)$, $(2,60)$, $(3,90)$ and use the graph to find the miles for $4$ gallons. Answer: $120$ miles.

problemArchetypes.name: Unit rate / better buy
problemArchetypes.example: A $12$-ounce bottle costs $\$3.00$ and a $20$-ounce bottle costs $\$4.40$. Which is the better buy? Compare $\$0.25$ per ounce to $\$0.22$ per ounce; the $20$-ounce bottle is the better buy.

problemArchetypes.name: Constant-speed distance-rate-time
problemArchetypes.example: A train travels $180$ miles in $3$ hours at a constant speed. At this rate, how far does it travel in $5$ hours? Unit rate $60$ mph, so $300$ miles.

problemArchetypes.name: Find the whole from a part and a percent
problemArchetypes.example: $15$ is $25\%$ of what number? Since $25\% = \frac{1}{4}$, the whole is $15\times 4 = 60$.

problemArchetypes.name: Measurement unit conversion by ratio
problemArchetypes.example: Convert $5$ feet to inches using the ratio $\frac{12 \text{ in}}{1 \text{ ft}}$: $5\times 12 = 60$ inches.

Easy.description: Single-step ratio or rate reasoning with friendly whole numbers. The unit rate is a whole number or the table extends by simple scaling. Percents are benchmark percents ($10\%$, $25\%$, $50\%$) of multiples that divide evenly. Conversions use one familiar factor in the direction that multiplies. tier1 starts here.
constraints: All quantities are whole numbers; the unit rate divides evenly (e.g. $\frac{180}{3}=60$)
Equivalent ratios scale by a whole-number multiplier ($\times 2$, $\times 3$, $\times 4$)
Percent of a quantity uses benchmark percents ($10\%, 25\%, 50\%, 100\%$) yielding whole-number results
One conversion factor, larger-to-smaller unit so you multiply (feet to inches, hours to minutes)
One reasoning tool suffices (a short table or a single division)

Medium.description: Two-step reasoning or a non-integer unit rate. Student computes a unit rate then scales to a requested value, compares two unit rates for a better buy, finds a non-benchmark percent, or finds the whole from a part. Decimals (money) appear. Both tier1 (upper end) and tier2 (lower end) live here.
constraints: Unit rate is a decimal that still terminates (e.g. $\$0.25$ per ounce), then scaled
Better-buy comparisons requiring two unit-rate computations
Find the whole given a part and a percent (reverse percent)
Conversions in the dividing direction (smaller-to-larger unit) or chained tables

Hard.description: Multi-step problems that combine tools or require setting up the ratio from a richer description before solving. Includes mixing two rates, multi-step percent (percent then add/subtract), reading a value off a graph or double number line and using it, or a conversion combined with a rate. tier2 ends here.
constraints: Three or more steps, or two different ratio tools used together
Set up the ratio from a multi-sentence context before computing
Percent increase/decrease or successive percents (e.g. find $20\%$ then subtract)
Combine a unit-rate computation with a unit conversion (e.g. miles per hour into miles per minute)
Compare three options, or interpret a point on a graph/double number line and extend it

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Treats the ratio as additive instead of multiplicative when extending a table
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $2:5$ scaled to $8$ sugar, adds $6$ to both parts giving $8:11$ (so flour $= 11$) instead of multiplying by $4$ to get $20$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Inverts the unit rate (divides the wrong quantity by the other)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $180$ miles in $3$ hours computes $\frac{3}{180}=\frac{1}{60}$ hours per mile and reports $60$ for the wrong unit, or uses it as if it were mph

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Chooses the lower total price as the better buy without finding the unit rate
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks the $\$3.00$ bottle over the $\$4.40$ bottle because $\$3.00 < \$4.40$, ignoring price per ounce

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Reads percent as a count rather than a rate per $100$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $30\%$ of $80$ answers $30$ (the percent number itself) instead of $\frac{30}{100}\times 80 = 24$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Takes the part as the whole in a reverse-percent problem
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For '$15$ is $25\%$ of what number?' answers $\frac{25}{100}\times 15 = 3.75$ instead of $15\div\frac{1}{4}=60$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Converts units in the wrong direction (multiplies when it should divide or vice versa)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Converts $60$ inches to feet by multiplying $60\times 12 = 720$ instead of dividing by $12$ to get $5$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses the two coordinates when plotting or reading a ratio graph
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Plots $(30,1)$ instead of $(1,30)$ for the rate $30$ miles per gallon, so reads off the wrong value

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Scales only one quantity in an equivalent ratio
commonMisconceptions.distractor: From $2:5$, doubles only the first term to get $4:5$ instead of $4:10$
